q: Risk-averse investors demanding a large equity risk premium are most likely expecting their future consumption outcomes and equity returns to be:
why:
B is correct. If investors demand high equity risk premiums, they are likely expecting their future consumption and equity returns to be positively correlated. The positive correlation indicates that equities will exhibit poor hedging properties, because equity returns will be high (i.e., pay off) during “good times” and will be low (i.e., not pay off) during “bad times.” In other words, the covariance between risk-averse investors’ inter-temporal rates of substitution and the expected future prices of equities is highly negative, resulting in a positive and large equity risk premium. This is the case because in good times, when equity returns are high, the marginal value of consumption is low. Similarly, in bad times, when equity returns are low, the marginal value of consumption is high. Holding all else constant, the larger the magnitude of the negative covariance term, the larger the risk premium

Which of the following financial assets is likely to offer the most effective hedge against bad consumption outcomes?


A. Equities.
Not Selected

Correct answer: 


B. Short-dated, default-free government bonds.


C. Long-dated, default-free government bonds.
Not Selected
Feedback
B is correct. The relative certainty about the real payoff from short-dated, default-free government bonds and, therefore, the relative certainty about the amount of consumption that the investor will be able to undertake with the payoff indicate that an investment in such bonds would be a good hedge against bad consumption outcomes

When assessing investment opportunities in equities, investors should:


A. assign higher equity risk premiums to non-cyclical companies, relative to cyclical companies.
Not Selected


B. forecast lower volatility in the growth rate of earnings for cyclical companies, relative to non-cyclical companies.
Not Selected

Correct answer: 


C. forecast higher growth rates in earnings for cyclical companies coming out of a recession, relative to non-cyclical companies.
Feedback
C is correct. During recessions, cyclical companies are likely to experience sharp declines in earnings, more so than non-cyclical companies. In contrast, while coming out of a recession, cyclical companies are likely to generate higher earnings growth relative to non-cyclical companies.

q: Other things equal, equilibrium price-to-earnings ratios (P/Es) will most likely decrease if:
options: there is less uncertainty about future inflation.
why: B is correct. Other things being equal, an increase in inflation expectations would result in lower equity prices relative to current earnings. This would result in lower equilibrium P/Es.

q: Which of the following statements relating to commercial real estate is correct?
options: Rental income from commercial real estate is generally unstable across business cycles.
Commercial real estate investments generally offer a good hedge against bad consumption outcomes.
The key difference in the discount rates applied to the cash flows of equity investments and commercial real estate investments relates to liquidity.
why: C is correct. To arrive at an appropriate discount rate to be used to discount the cash flows from a commercial real estate investment, a liquidity premium is added to the discount rate applicable to equity investments. The added liquidity premium provides additional compensation for the risk that the real estate investment may be very illiquid in bad economic times

q: Which of the following statements regarding applications of ETFs in portfolio management is correct?
options: Equity ETFs tend to be more active than fixed-income ETFs.
The range of risk exposures available in the futures market is more diverse than that available in the ETF space.
ETFs that have the highest trading volumes in their asset class category are generally preferred for tactical trading applications.
why: C is correct. ETFs that have the highest trading volumes in their asset class category are generally preferred for tactical trading applications.

q: A non-dividend-paying stock currently trades at $55.25. The annual interest rate is 3.75% with annual compounding. Using the no-arbitrage approach, the equilibrium 6-month forward price is closest to:
why: A. Incorrect because it divides the spot price by the interest rate (instead of multiplying) to arrive at the forward rate, or = F0 = FV(S0) = $55.25 / (1 + 3.75%)0.5 ≈ $54.24. | B. Correct because S0 = $55.25, r = 3.75% and T = 6/12 = 0.5, and F0 = FV(S0) = S0(1 + r)T = $55.25 × (1 + 3.75%)0.5 ≈ $56.28, where S0 = spot price at the initiation date, r = annually compounded interest rate, T = time to maturity in years, F0 = forward price at the initiation date, and FV = future value function. If we assume annual compounding (r), then FV(S0) = S0(1 + r)T. | C. Incorrect because it does not incorporate the six-month maturity when calculating the interest rate to arrive at the forward rate, or = F0 = FV(S0) = $55.25 × (1 + 3.75%) ≈ $57.32.

q:
An analyst gathers the following information about a stock and its underlying cash flows:
Current stock price	$95.00
Dividend to be paid in 3 months	$4.25
Annual interest rate with annual compounding	5.30%
Using the no-arbitrage approach, the equilibrium 11-month forward price is closest to:
why: A. Incorrect because it calculates the benefit of the dividend for the entire 11 months, or F0 = FV(S0) – FV(D) = $95 (1 + 0.053)11/12 – $4.25 (1 + 0.053)11/12 = $99.6054 – $4.4560 ≈ $95.15. | B. Correct because S0 = $95, r = 5.3% (annual compounding), and T = 11/12, and after 3 months, we will receive the benefit of a $4.25 dividend, which earns interest for (11 – 3) = 8 months. Therefore, F0 = FV(S0) – FV(D) = $95 (1 + 0.053)11/12 – $4.25 (1 + 0.053)8/12 = $99.6054 – $4.3989 ≈ $95.21. | C. Incorrect because it calculates the benefit of the dividend for only 3 months, or F0 = FV(S0) – FV(D) = $95 (1 + 0.053)11/12 – $4.25 (1 + 0.053)3/12 = $99.6054 – $4.3052 ≈ $95.30.

q: An equity forward has a remaining maturity of six months. A dividend payment is announced before the forward's expiration date. If the news announcement does not change the underlying price, the forward value will most likely:
why: A. Correct because the old forward price is fixed. The discounted difference in the new forward price and the old forward price is the value. If we impose a new dividend, it would lower the new forward price and thus decrease the value of the old forward contract. | B. Incorrect because the old forward price is fixed. The discounted difference in the new forward price and the old forward price is the value. If we impose a new dividend, it would lower the new forward price and thus decrease, not keep the same, the value of the old forward contract. | C. Incorrect because the old forward price is fixed. The discounted difference in the new forward price and the old forward price is the value. If we impose a new dividend, it would lower the new forward price and thus decrease, not increase, the value of the old forward contract.

q:
A 1-year plain vanilla interest rate swap has semiannual resets. The fixed swap rate is 5.2% and the subsequent floating MRRs through the life of the contract are given as follows:
Time	6-Month MRR (Annualized) Observed at Time t
t = 0	5.0%
t = 6 months	4.8%
t = 12 months	5.4%
If the 30/360 day count method is used, the pay-fixed, receive-floating net cash flow at t = 6 months is closest to:
why: A. Incorrect because this neglects the fact that the floating interest rate is set in advance and settled in arrears, i.e., it uses the MRR at t = 6 months rather than the MRR at t = 0; 0.5 × (0.048 – 0.052) = –0.002. This is also the value if the cash flow is stated on an annual basis. | B. Correct because the convention in the swap market is that the floating interest rate is assumed to be advanced set and settled in arrears; thus, rFLT,i (the floating-leg rate) is set at the beginning of the period and paid at the end. Therefore, the appropriate floating rate to use for the 6-month cash flow is the MRR at t = 0, i.e., 5.0%. Moreover, the pay-fixed, receive-floating net cash flow can be expressed as AP × (rFLT,i – rFIX), where rFIX is the swap's fixed rate and AP denotes the accrual period, which accounts for the payment frequency and day count methods. Since the 30/360 day count method is assumed and the payment frequency is semi-annual, AP = 180/360 = 0.5. Therefore, the net cash flow at t = 6 months, for every unit of the notional amount, is 0.5 × (0.050 – 0.052) = –0.001. | C. Incorrect because this is the net cash flow at t = 6 months for a receive-fixed, pay-floating swap, not a pay-fixed, received-floating swap (i.e., it is the negative of the correct cash flow). It is also the answer if the MRR at t = 12 months is used rather than the MRR at t = 0; 0.5 × (0.054 – 0.052) = 0.001 per unit notional.

q: Which of the following is not an assumption made when using replication with bonds to price a plain vanilla interest rate swap at initiation? The value of the floating-rate bond at initiation should be equal to:
options: the value of the fixed-rate bond.
why: A. Correct because pricing the swap means to determine the rate (rFIX) such that the value of the swap [not the floating-rate bond] at initiation is zero. Said differently, to price the swap, the value of the fixed-rate bond must equal the value of the floating-rate bond. Moreover, the value of a floating-rate bond at the reset date (including initiation) is 1 (par) because the interest payment is set to match the discount rate. Recall that when the YTM (discount rate) of a bond is equal to the coupon rate, the bond sells at par. | B. Incorrect because the value of a floating-rate bond at the reset date (including initiation) is 1 (par) because the interest payment is set to match the discount rate. Recall that when the YTM (discount rate) of a bond is equal to the coupon rate, the bond sells at par. | C. Incorrect because, to price the swap, the value of the fixed-rate bond must equal the value of the floating-rate bond.

q:
Sixty days ago, a European company entered into a receive-fixed GBP, pay-fixed EUR swap with the following specifications:
Swap notional amount (exchanged at initiation and maturity)	EUR 5 million
Original swap term	1 year, with quarterly resets
Fixed swap rate (at initiation) in EUR	4.55%
Fixed swap rate (at initiation) in GBP	5.28%
GBP/EUR spot exchange rate at initiation (amount of GBP per 1 EUR)	0.88
Currently, long positions in the associated bonds with unit face value are priced at EUR 0.97 and GBP 1.06, respectively. If the current exchange rate is 0.91 GBP/EUR, the value of the swap to the European company is closest to:
why: A. Correct because the value of a fixed-for-fixed currency swap at some future point in time, say Time t, is simply the difference in a pair of fixed-rate bonds, one expressed in currency a [here GBP] and one expressed in currency b [here EUR]. To express the bonds in the same currency units, we convert the currency b bond into units of currency a through a spot foreign exchange transaction at a new rate St. The value of a 'receive currency a, pay currency b' (fixed-for-fixed) swap at any time t expressed in terms of currency a is the difference in bond values: VCS = Va – StVb. Moreover, the NA (or par value) of the bond denominated in currency a (NAa) must equal the spot exchange rate S0 times the notional amount (or par value) of the bond denominated in currency b (NAb). That is, NAa = S0 × NAb = 0.88 × 5,000,000 = GBP 4,400,000. Finally, the value of each fixed-rate bond can be computed by multiplying the notional amount in that currency by the value of a long position in a bond with face value equal to one unit of that currency (the values given in the question). Hence, VCS = (4,400,000 × 1.06) – [0.91 × (5,000,000 × 0.97)] = 4,664,000 – 4,413,500 = GBP 250,500. | B. Incorrect because it uses the exchange rate at initiation, rather than after 60 days, to convert the EUR fixed-rate bond value to GBP, yielding: VCS = (4,400,000 × 1.06) – [0.88 × (5,000,000 × 0.97)] = 4,664,000 – 4,268,000 = GBP 396,000. | C. Incorrect because it misinterprets the stated exchange rates as EUR per GBP, rather than GBP per EUR, i.e., concluding that S0 = 1/0.88 = 1.1363636 (GBP/EUR) and St = 1/0.91 = 1.0989011 (GBP/EUR). This yields: NAa = S0 × NAb = 1.1363636 × 5,000,000 = GBP 5,681,818 and VCS = (5,681,818 × 1.06) – [1.0989011 × (5,000,000 × 0.97)] ≈ 6,022,727 – 5,329,670 = GBP 693,057.

q:
An analyst gathers the following market quotations for spot market reference rates up to one year:
Maturity (Months)	 Rate
3	2.30%
6	2.50%
9	2.70%
12	3.00%
Assuming a 30/360 day count, the no-arbitrage fixed rate on a new 9 × 12 forward rate agreement (FRA) is closest to:
why: A. Incorrect because it is simply the quoted market spot rate for three months (2.30%) from the table, instead of deriving the forward rate from the 9-month and 12-month spot rates. | B. Incorrect because it is calculated as the simple arithmetic average of the 9-month spot rate and the 12-month spot rate, i.e., (2.70% + 3.00%)/2 = 2.85%. | C. Correct because the FRA is created and priced at Time 0, the initiation date, and expires h days later. The underlying instrument has m days to maturity as of the FRA expiration date. We derive the forward rate (or FRA rate, FRA0) from two spot rates (such as MRR): the longer rate LT and the shorter rate Lh. FRA0 = {[1 + LTtT]/[1 + Lhth] – 1}/tm FRA0 = {[1 + 3.00%]/[1 + 2.70% × (9/12)] – 1}/(3/12) ≈ 3.82%

q: A company entered into a 2-year receive-equity, pay-fixed swap three months ago, where the notional amount of both legs is €5.0 million. If the equity stock price at swap initiation was €50 and the current fair value of the fixed leg of the swap is €5.3 million, the current break-even equity price for the swap is closest to:
why: A. Incorrect because the break-even equity price for the swap is the price at which the net fair value of the swap equals 0, hence the value of the receive-equity leg should equal €5.3 million. If the current equity price was €47, the value of the receive-equity leg would be (€47/€50) × €5.0 million = €4.7 million, not €5.3 million. | B. Incorrect because the break-even equity price for the swap is the price at which the net fair value of the swap equals 0, hence the value of the receive-equity leg should equal €5.3 million. If the current equity price was €50, the value of the receive-equity leg would be (€50/€50) × €5.0 million = €5.0 million, not €5.3 million. | C. Correct because the break-even equity price for the swap is the price at which the net fair value of the swap equals 0, hence the value of the receive-equity leg should equal €5.3 million. The current break-even equity price is such that the value of the receive-equity leg is (X/€50) × €5.0 million = €5.3 million. Hence, X = €5.3 million/€5.0 million × €50 = €53.

q:
An analyst gathers the following information about a bond futures contract and the underlying semiannual pay bond:
Clean bond price	103
Coupon rate	3.00%
Days since last coupon	55
Days until next coupon	125
Conversion factor	0.75
Days until futures contract expiry	30
Annualized 1-month risk-free rate	3.25%
If the quoted futures price is 138, based on the carry arbitrage model this futures contract is:
why: A. Incorrect because the quoted futures price is greater than the equilibrium futures price; hence, the futures contract is overvalued rather than undervalued based on its quoted price. | B. Incorrect because the quoted futures price is greater than the equilibrium futures price; hence, the futures contract is overvalued rather than fairly valued based on its quoted price. | C. Correct because, according to the carry arbitrage model, Q0 = [1/CF] {FV[B0 + AI0] – AIT – FVCI}, where CF = Conversion factor, B0 = Clean bond price, AI0 = Accrued interest at value date, AIT = Accrued interest at futures expiration, and FVCI = Future value of coupons paid. Accrued interest at value date: AI0 = [55/(55 + 125)] × 3% × 100/2 = 0.458 Accrued interest at futures expiration: AIT = [(30 + 55)/(55 + 125)] × 3% × 100/2 = 0.708 FV[B0 + AI0] = (103 + 0.458) × (1 + 3.25%)30/360 = 103.734 Substituting: Q0 = [1/0.75] {103.734 – 0.708 – 0} = 137.37 The quoted futures price of 138 is greater than the equilibrium futures price of 137.37; thus, the futures contract is overvalued.
